Astyanax. The infant son of Hector and Andromache, prince of Troy who never reached manhood. He was caught in war he could not comprehend, and his fate symbolizes Troy's ultimate destruction. After the city falls, his death becomes emblematic of the war's cruelty and the erasure of Troy's future.

His name Astyanax means lord of the city in Greek. He was also called Scamandrius after the river near Troy. These titles of hope and promise were ones his short life would never fulfill. Born into the royal Trojan family during the decade-long war, he appears in the Iliad only briefly. Most memorably, he appears in the scene where his father Hector says goodbye to his family before battle. In that scene, he was famously frightened by his father's war helmet and its Gorgon plume, crying in his nurse's arms. A poignant image showing the human cost of war and innocence confronted with symbols of violence.

His fate was sealed when Troy fell after the wooden horse strategy. Accounts vary on his death. Some say Achilles's son Pyrrhus threw him from the walls. Others name Achilles directly or Menelaus. His death was considered particularly abhorrent even by ancient standards, representing the Greeks' ruthless and deliberate elimination of Troy's entire royal lineage to prevent future revenge or challenges to Greek dominance.

His mother Andromache was left without husband or son, becoming a captive and slave after his death. She was forced to serve Pyrrhus and later pass to Helenus, symbolizing the total destruction of her family. Later Roman tradition, particularly in Virgil's Aeneid, posthumously gives Astyanax a son named Ascanius who escapes Troy with Aeneas and becomes the progenitor of Rome. A mythological bridge linking Trojan destiny to Roman greatness.

His father was Hector, the greatest Trojan warrior, whose death in combat precedes and leaves Astyanax defenseless. His mother Andromache's grief and mourning of both defines her character and becomes emblematic of war's cost on women. His story appears in the Iliad, the epic poem marking his innocence against warfare. The Trojan War, the decade-long conflict, defined and ultimately ended his short existence. Troy, the city-state whose future and lineage died with his murder by the Greeks. Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior whose son Pyrrhus threw him from the walls.
